episodes.title: The Missing Infrastructure for AI Agents: Documents | Reducto’s Adit Abraham
episodes.about: AI agents can reason over enormous amounts of information, but much of the world's actual work is still trapped in PDFs, spreadsheets, scans, and other formats that models struggle to reliably understand. Reducto co-founder and CEO Adit Abraham argues that solving this document layer is essential if agents are going to take on consequential work in healthcare, legal, finance, and insurance. He explains why traditional OCR breaks down on messy real-world documents, how Reducto combines vision-language models with specialized infrastructure, and why frontier models can silently drop information on long extraction tasks. Reducto now processes billions of pages each month.
episodes.why: Out today: agents can reason, but the world's work sits in PDFs and scans - Reducto's Adit Abraham on the document layer, why OCR breaks on messy files, and frontier models silently dropping data on long extractions.

episodes.title: Why AI Companies Are Betting Personality Beats Intelligence
episodes.about: As AI models become more capable, personality is becoming a competitive battleground. From the GPT-4o backlash to Meta's Muse and ChatGPT's Dots, NLW explores why how an AI feels to use could increasingly determine which products win - and which models work best for different tasks. In the headlines: Musk's SpaceX share pledge for American children, export controls as leverage over AI labs, and the federal DeepSeek ban.
episodes.why: Personality is becoming the battleground: the GPT-4o backlash, Meta's Muse and ChatGPT's Dots - plus the SpaceX share pledge, export controls as leverage over AI labs, and the federal DeepSeek ban.

episodes.title: AI is dividing the math world in two
episodes.about: Over the last several months, the AI industry has set its sights on some of the problems that have stymied mathematicians for years. In some cases, AI models have made huge progress - though exactly how much isn't always obvious. The Verge's Robert Hart explains what OpenAI and others have actually accomplished, the disastrously bad ways the companies have interacted with researchers, and whether there's a future left for human mathematics.
episodes.why: AI models are cracking problems that stumped mathematicians for years - Robert Hart separates the real progress from the hype and the labs' messy dealings with researchers.

episodes.title: A World Model of Life: Biohub's Alex Rives on Virtual Cells, Measurement, & the $1.8B Data Push
episodes.about: Alex Rives, Head of Science at Biohub and former lead of the ESM protein language model project, joins Nathan to discuss Biohub's mission to construct a predictive world model of life. Supported by an expanded $1.8 billion Virtual Biology Initiative alongside partners including the Department of Energy, NIH, Google DeepMind, and Meta, Rives outlines the push to map contextual cellular biology across hundreds of billions of cells. He breaks down why today's AI architectures fall short of simulating true virtual cells, and the path toward an information-level cell model within five years - ultimately shifting medicine from traditional drugs to programmable interventions.
episodes.why: Biohub's Alex Rives, of ESM fame, on building a predictive world model of life: the $1.8B Virtual Biology Initiative, hundreds of billions of cells, and why today's architectures cannot yet simulate a virtual cell.

episodes.title: How easy is it to game AI search results?
episodes.about: More and more people are turning to chatbots to search the web. But researchers are finding these systems can be gamed. Marketplace called up Xiyang Hu, an assistant professor at Arizona State University who leads the Generative Learning and Augmented Decision Lab, to explain how AI chatbot search results can be manipulated - including a query-agnostic black-box attack study presented at ICML, and new research showing language models often favor their own text.
episodes.why: Discovery pick - APM's daily tech show, in short form: as search moves to chatbots, ASU's Xiyang Hu explains how researchers game AI search results, and the new bias of models favoring their own text.
